articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026, targeting five individuals, four entities, and nine vessels involved in facilitating Iranian commodity exports as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast.' The targeted entities include a Panama- and Greece-based law firm, shipping agents in Singapore and the UAE, and vessels linked to Iran's 'shadow fleet' for transporting petroleum, petrochemicals, and other commodities.

Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. The action also included the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, along with amended Frequently Asked Questions to provide further guidance on the updated sanctions landscape.

These measures aim to disrupt corporate structures and logistics services used to conceal beneficial ownership and evade sanctions, particularly those imposed under Executive Order 13902, which targets designated sectors of the Iranian economy.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Middle East Eye

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations on Chinese Entities for Intellectual Property Theft
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026, targeting five Chinese technology and investment businesses. These entities are linked to the theft of Google's artificial intelligence secrets, marking an unusual application of sanctions legislation to combat intellectual property theft.

Among the designated entities are Shanghai Zhisuan Technology, founded by former Google engineer Linwei Ding, and Beijing-based investment business MiraclePlus, along with three associated investment entities. Ding is accused of stealing over 2,000 pages of confidential material related to Google's AI systems between May 2022 and April 2023.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing transactions pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and an updated Frequently Asked Question on October 16, 2026. This action follows recent diplomatic shifts and ongoing discussions between the U.S. and Venezuela regarding energy pacts.

The specific details of the amendments were not immediately disclosed but are expected to provide further guidance on authorized transactions and activities involving Venezuela. This comes shortly after the removal of a prominent Venezuelan official from the SDN list.
These adjustments reflect the evolving U.S. policy towards Venezuela, which has seen a pivot from economic warfare to increased engagement, particularly concerning the country's oil sector.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities and a Cuban Bank, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to target Iran's international financial networks and its 'shadow banking architecture,' as well as to increase pressure on Cuba's state-run entities.

Specifically, the U.S. Department of State designated Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA), a Cuban state-run bank, pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 14404. This designation aims to further restrict Cuba's access to international financial systems.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on authorized transactions and activities. These measures underscore the Trump administration's intensified pressure campaign on Cuba and its continued focus on disrupting Iran's illicit financial activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan Legislator Jorge Rodriguez from Sanctions List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of Jorge Rodriguez, the head of Venezuela's National Assembly, from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) blacklist on October 14, 2026. This move signifies a notable shift in U.S. policy towards Venezuela, following earlier sanctions relief for other key figures.

Rodriguez, who has led the Venezuelan legislature since 2021, was sanctioned under the Trump administration due to his ministerial roles. His delisting unblocks his assets subject to U.S. jurisdiction and lifts restrictive personal measures.

This decision comes amidst broader U.S.-Venezuela energy pacts and diplomatic talks, with analysts viewing it as a strategic effort to intensify institutional stability and facilitate foreign debt restructuring, as well as to open pathways for international energy companies in Venezuela's oil sector.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cartel del Noreste Facilitators in Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Action
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities supporting the Cartel del Noreste (CDN) in Mexico. This action aims to disrupt the cartel's financial and operational networks.

The designations include Gamaliel Garza Elias and Gamaliel Garza Garcia, along with several entities in Mexico involved in horse racing, construction, and asphalt products. These businesses, such as CONSTRUCCIONES Y EDIFICACIONES GARZA ELIAS, S.A. DE C.V., CUADRA SAN DIBANH, and CONCRETOS Y PRODUCTOS ASFALTICOS DEL NORTE, S.A. DE C.V., were identified as supporting the CDN's illicit activities.

These designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating transnational criminal organizations and their facilitators, particularly those involved in narcotics trafficking and activities that pose a threat to national security.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates International Criminal Court, Issues General Licenses, Removes Burma Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the designation of the International Criminal Court (ICC) on October 9, 2026, as part of a broader U.S. campaign against the tribunal. This action was accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.

The U.S. government has accused the ICC of politicization and unfairly targeting Americans and allies, including Israel, for war crime charges. The sanctions aim to block any ICC assets in U.S. jurisdictions and require U.S. companies or individuals to wind down business with the court within six months.

Concurrently, OFAC also announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics and a Burma-related designation removal. The designation of the ICC has drawn strong condemnation from the international legal community and the United Nations, who view it as an assault on the rule of law and international justice.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This action follows recent developments in U.S. policy regarding sanctions on Russia.

The new General License, identified as GL 135, authorizes certain transactions related to the sale, delivery, offloading, and importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel into the United States until April 7, 2027. This move is intended to help bring down global energy prices.

This issuance comes amidst a complex sanctions landscape, where the U.S. administration has recently waived many Russia-related sanctions and tariffs introduced by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New Iran and Amended Russia General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026, as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting Iran's 'shadow fleet network.' This action intensifies U.S. pressure on entities facilitating illicit funding and trade for the Iranian regime.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License. These measures aim to provide specific authorizations while maintaining pressure on both regimes.

The Iran-related designations are part of a broader strategy to disrupt the Iranian regime's revenue streams and its support for terrorist proxies, while the amended Russia-related General License reflects ongoing adjustments to sanctions policy in response to global energy dynamics.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $11,662,930. The settlement, announced on October 13, 2026, addresses 475 apparent violations of various sanctions programs.

These violations included transactions related to Iran, Russia, Belarus, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. The settlement is part of a broader enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC.
The penalties stem from the bank's failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks and deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act/anti-money laundering (BSA/AML) compliance program.

articles.headline: EU Adds Individuals and Entities to DPRK Sanctions List Over Weapons Programs and Russia Ties
body: The European Council adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) on October 12, 2026. These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities contributing to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically address activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

Among those sanctioned is Ri Song Jin, a researcher at the DPRK National Aerospace Technology Administration, deployed to Russia as a technician supporting Russia's use of DPRK missiles. The Council also listed Russian real estate development company Samolet Group and its CEO, Anna Nikolaevna Akinshina, for their involvement.

articles.headline: Cuba Accuses U.S. of Threatening Nations Ahead of UN Embargo Vote
body: Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions, and other retaliatory measures to influence their votes on an upcoming United Nations resolution calling for an end to the long-running U.S. embargo against the island. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez stated on October 21, 2026, that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the U.S. ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, are personally leading this campaign.

The UN General Assembly has historically voted overwhelmingly in favor of resolutions condemning the U.S. economic embargo, which has been in place for over six decades. Cuba argues that the embargo has exacerbated economic hardship, leading to shortages of basic goods, crumbling infrastructure, and rampant inflation.

Rodriguez described the alleged U.S. actions as a 'new and dangerous way of conducting multilateral diplomacy,' reflecting what he termed the 'impotence' of the U.S. in the face of international opposition to its embargo.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Significant Enforcement Actions Against Major Banks for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced significant enforcement actions for October 2026, including civil money penalties against American Express National Bank and Bank of America, National Association. American Express National Bank was assessed a $350 million penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports (SARs), and violations related to customer due diligence and customer identification programs.

Bank of America, National Association, received a $750 million civil money penalty for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, untimely SAR filings, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. These actions highlight the OCC's commitment to ensuring banks maintain robust anti-money laundering controls.

Additionally, the OCC issued Orders of Prohibition against two institution-affiliated parties: Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at Fifth Third Bank, N.A., for embezzling approximately $292,000 in customer funds, and Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at U.S. Bank National Association, for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
